text:
Non so ancora come dirlo senza piangere, quindi lo scrivo e basta. Il 14 marzo è morto a Bologna mio padre, Giovanni Rossetti. Aveva 78 anni e per quarant'anni ha guidato la sua vecchia Fiat Panda targata GE 482 KL per portare pane e giornali a tutto il quartiere di San Donato. Chi lo conosceva sa che non passava mai davanti al Bar Centrale senza entrare a salutare Marisa, e che ogni mattina alle sette era già lì a leggere il quotidiano con il suo caffè macchiato.

Con mia madre Lucia, con mio fratello Paolo e con me, papà è stato un uomo tranquillo ma ostinato. Andava in palestra alla Palestra Olimpia tre volte a settimana fino all'ultimo, e diceva che il segreto era non saltare mai il lunedì. Ha lottato a lungo con la malattia al Policlinico Sant'Orsola, dove i medici e le infermiere lo hanno trattato con una gentilezza che non dimenticheremo. Il funerale si terrà sabato 22 marzo alle ore 10 nella chiesa di San Donato.

Chi vuole ricordarlo può scrivere su Instagram al profilo @giovanni.rossetti.ricordo, dove stiamo raccogliendo le foto della sua vita. Grazie a tutti, davvero. Ciao papà, ti voglio bene. Giovanni, sempre con noi.

text:
I have been asked to say a few words about my father, Tomasz Wiśniewski, and I have to admit that I have started this speech more times than I can count. Every draft felt too small. How do you fit a man who left Kraków at nineteen with one suitcase and a borrowed coat into a few minutes at a lectern? My name is Anna Wiśniewski, and I am his daughter, and I am still trying to understand how much of him I was lucky enough to inherit.

He moved to Toronto in 1989, a few months before the wall came down, and he always said he had chosen the wrong year to leave and the right decision anyway. The first winter was hard. He worked nights at a bakery on Roncesvalles and studied English from a battered grammar book he carried everywhere, even into the shower, which my mother found hilarious. He never lost his accent, and he never tried to. He told me once that the accent was the only thing nobody could take from him, and that he was proud of every syllable.

When I think about the years after we settled, I think about Marek Dąbrowski, who arrived in Canada the same spring as my father and became his closest friend. They fixed up old bicycles together in our garage and argued about football, politics and whether pierogi should ever contain cheese. Marek was there in the hospital in March, sitting quietly in the corner with a thermos of tea, and it was Marek who sat with my father when the rest of us had gone home to sleep. My dad would have wanted me to say his name today.

He was never a man of grand gestures. He showed love by making sure the car was warm before we got in, by remembering that I hated the crust on my sandwiches, by calling every Sunday from the same phone at the same time for twenty-two years, even after I moved to Vancouver. The last time I saw him, he asked me whether I was eating properly, and I rolled my eyes, and he laughed the way he always did, with his whole chest.

So this is my goodbye, Tata. Thank you for the suitcase, for the coat, for the bread you baked in the dark, and for the courage it took to start over twice in one life. I will keep speaking your words in my own accent, and I will keep your Sunday phone calls alive in the way I call my own daughter. Rest now. You earned it.

I've known Noa since we were nineteen and shared a terrible apartment on Ben Yehuda Street in Jerusalem, where the water heater only worked on Tuesdays. Back then she was studying nursing at Hadassah, double shifts and all, and still somehow the only person I knew who could make a cold kitchen feel like home. Ever since, she has been the steady one, the friend who drives across the country at midnight when you call. Tonight I get to say what we all know: Noa, you were made for someone patient, funny, and a little bit stubborn, and Yoni, you're the lucky one. Mazel tov to you both.

text: Hi all, I moved from Lisbon to Toronto about six months ago and I'm finding it really hard to make friends here. My dog Biscuit keeps me getting out to the park every morning, but nobody talks to me there. I've been going to the Maple Leaf Cafe on Dundas for my usual oat latte and the staff are lovely, but it's still just small talk. My cousin Inês said to try a class, so I signed up for pottery at Clay & Co. starting March 14 and I'm nervous. Has anyone here made the move from Portugal or elsewhere in Europe and found their way into a social circle? Any tips for a shy person would mean a lot. Thanks in advance, Inês's cousin Rafael
